body: Developed through an ongoing collaboration since 2012, Forward, March! by Maria Andersson and Nancy Atakan examines the influence of Swedish physical culture on Turkey’s modernization process in the early twentieth century. Centered around educator and sports reformer Selim Sırrı Tarcan and the lives of his daughters Selma Mimaroğlu and Azade Kent, the exhibition explores the relationship between physical education, choreography, gender, and the construction of modern identity.

Wooden bars, used by athletes for various warm-up exercises and performances, serve as the base for the exhibition furniture; canvas prints of the main text, drawings by artists, and videos displayed on different types of screens are placed on scaled versions of these wooden bars.

Bringing together videos, textiles, drawings, photographs, and archival materials, the exhibition traces how bodily movement became a tool for social transformation and women’s emancipation in Turkey. Moving between historical research and speculative narration, the works unfold connections between gymnastics, dance, folklore, and collective memory.
The adaptation of Maria Andersson’s work Anthem into an interactive book format is installed in a circular arrangement around the columns.

Are pedestals or display cases only meant to hold artworks? Does their life end when the exhibition closes, or can they assume different roles with each use—becoming both support structures and design objects in their own right? Tracing display units produced for SALT's programs and repurposed on various occasions, Trash explores material decisions within exhibition-making processes. It offers a multilayered perspective on scenography and design practices through objects left behind from past exhibitions. Drawing on the institution’s 15-year history, the program opens up a discussion on the circulation of materials from gallery space to storage, the often-invisible exhibition infrastructures, and diverse forms of reuse.

These materials—neither the output of an industrial production line nor readily defined as “waste”—may gradually be written off and come to be considered “trash” while awaiting new functions in storage. Taking this nuance between waste and trash as a point of departure, the program underscores that value is not inherent in the material itself, but rather emerges from the context in which it is used and the meanings attributed to it. By assembling a pile of materials, the installation sets a stage that reveals the transience and mutability of this context, while also highlighting the exhibitionary conventions shaped by institutional decisions.

Transforming SALT Beyoğlu’s ground floor into a production space, where materials such as wood, glass, plexiglass, metal, foam, and paper are sorted, modified, and repurposed, Trash shows that discarded materials also carry memory and can hold archival qualities. Accompanied by workshops and talks on exhibition design practices, it revisits existing productions from new perspectives to develop proposals in dialogue with the space.

QR codes embedded within the materials connected visitors to SALT’s fifteen-year exhibition history and the exhibitions from which the materials originated, revealing the design logics, production methods, and material histories embedded within the institution’s exhibition practice.

Throughout the program, materials were transformed into new display structures, generating discussions on adaptive reuse within exhibition-making. In parallel, public talks with Ippolito Pestellini Laparelli, Carlos Mínguez Carrasco, Superpool, Can and Aslı Altay, and Aslı Çiçek broadened the discussion around exhibition design and scenography through different spatial and curatorial practices.

As Trash did not seek a final product, the installation itself remained intentionally open-ended. To sustain this ongoing discussion, Salt aims to build a network with the architecture and industrial design departments of the universities, developing structured routes for the material circulation and reuse of remnants generated by future projects. This vision found its first tangible expression on the final day of the program, which concluded with Aslı Çiçek’s talk: visitors claimed many of the raw materials and exhibition units that remained unused after the workshops, marking the first actual step toward a future of collective material sharing.

Originally presented at SALT in Istanbul, The 90s Onstage was reconfigured for its presentation at Kunstverein in Hamburg. Focusing on the notions of stage and performance, the exhibition brings together artistic productions from 1990s Turkey through archival materials, photographs, video works, and ephemera.

Retaining one of the defining elements of the original exhibition, this iteration unfolds around an elongated stage that extends throughout the gallery as a ramp, display surface, and viewing platform.

Each section is conceived as a compact installation composed of archival documents, artworks, slide projectors, CRT monitors, 4:3 video works, and subtle light interventions. At the center of this constellation, the stage-ramp emerges as a connective element, inviting visitors to re-enter the performances, encounters, and collective experiences that shaped 1990s Turkey.

Based on extensive research by artist Mike Bode and screenwriter Caner Yalçın, the exhibition exploring the fragmented history of Dark World, the 1953 film by Metin Erksan and Bedri Rahmi Eyüboğlu centered on the life of Âşık Veysel. Through archival materials, censored footage, altered scenes, and newly discovered film fragments, the exhibition examines how state ideology, censorship, and production processes reshaped the film’s narrative. Rather than reconstructing the “original” version, the project embraces the film’s fragmented condition to investigate the mechanisms of image-making, historical memory, and cultural representation in 1950s Turkey.

A hand-crafted animation constructs the exhibition’s visual identity through fragmented letters. Printed on transparent acetate sheets and assembled within a small slide viewer, the animation draws from the material qualities of film. The grain of the image, darkened edges, and isolated letterforms allude to the processes of editing and montage that underpin the exhibition’s investigation.

The minimal layout presents selected fragments from the film. One side of the space features sequences reflecting 1950s Turkey—scenes that were added during the censorship process and were not part of the film’s original version—alongside newly restored footage from the recently discovered print. All sequences remain silent, while the space is intermittently filled with the voice of Âşık Veysel in CRT monitors.

The pre-censored cut and the premiered version are still unknown, while the copies in circulation differ somewhat in sound, image, and editing. Adding to this fragmented legacy is a 35mm nitrate print, recently discovered in the archive of Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University Prof. Sami Şekeroğlu Cinema and Television Center, which includes footage unearthed for the first time.

The opposite side operates as a research laboratory, where the film’s original 1953 poster, a painting by Bedri Rahmi Eyüboğlu, censorship reports, and interviews with the researchers behind Dark World are assembled alongside the film’s final sequences unfolding in the background.

Screenwriter Caner Yalçın reconstructed and transcribed the multiple existing versions of Dark World. Printed materials displayed on a large central table reveal the differences between the scripts, while surrounding surfaces present archival material related to the film.

Notes on Air is an immersive installation conceived and designed by the Milan-based interdisciplinary design agency 2050+ for Salt Beyoğlu’s Forum. It stages a reimagination of air toxicity, employing a blend of material, sonic, and visual experiments. Through this aesthetic exploration, elements that are typically intangible—untouched, unheard, unseen—provide an instance for an embodied, sensorial encounter.

The installation encourages visitors to engage with the materiality of air as it unfolds through a series of interventions: curtains that reveal the chemical composition of air, each depicted with a color indicating different degrees of toxicity, alongside embroidered data and imagery demonstrating their prevalence across varying scales; a soundscape that conjures the otherwise inaudible conditions resulting from chemical reactions triggered by the interaction of these airborne elements; and an animated reconstruction of the Istanbul sky, crafted through photogrammetry, a technique typically used to capture static, solid objects. In this instance, it attempts to evidence and give form to the invisible gaseous substances that envelop the Earth.

An exhibition exploring performance culture in Turkey from the late 1980s to the early 2000s through archival materials, video works, objects, and ephemera. Tracing performances across clubs, parks, historical landmarks, and abandoned sites, the exhibition reconsiders the stage as a temporary space of encounter and collective experience.

The exhibition design invites visitors onto the stage from the moment they enter. Built from reused partition walls and covered in yellow-painted vinyl, an elongated ramp carries the rhythm of İstiklal Avenue into the gallery. Acting as a stage, display surface, and circulation route, it shows video works and archival materials linked to the street’s role as one of Istanbul’s busiest sites for performance and public life.

Seretonin I (1989) and Seretonin II (1992) turned industrial buildings awaiting redevelopment into temporary stages for artistic production. These exhibitions brought together installations, performances, music, and happenings. They activated spaces like Feshane and Yedikule Gashouse while encouraging interactions between artists, workers, and audiences. Organized collectively and open to participation, Seretonin became a key part of Istanbul’s alternative cultural scene in the 1990s. Drawing from these industrial settings, the exhibition design recreates the factory as a performance space on the upper floors. Metal structures create usable volumes that visitors can explore, while 4:3 video works are shown on CRT monitors hung at different heights, reflecting the spatial and material conditions of the original venues.

Founded and directed by Hüseyin Katırcıoğlu, the Assos Performing Arts Festival transformed the village of Behramkale and the ancient city of Assos into a stage throughout the second half of the 1990s. Drawing from the festival’s relationship with the landscape, photographs are distributed throughout the gallery at varying heights. Echoing the movement of artists and audiences across Assos, the images extend beyond a conventional display format and spread through the space as a dispersed visual field.


The section culminates with a series of movable costumes designed by Selçuk Gürışık for SALT. Referencing the costumes he created for the festival, these performative objects bring a bodily presence into an exhibition otherwise composed of archival traces and documentation.

Commissioned by SALT, CLIMAVORE: Seasons Made to Drift by Cooking Sections (Daniel Fernández Pascual and Alon Schwabe) explores how climate change reshapes food infrastructures, eating habits, and ecological relations. Through installations, archival materials, and spatial interventions, the exhibition traces emerging “seasons” shaped by drought, shifting ecosystems, industrial agriculture, and environmental transformation across Turkey and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Through selected cases, CLIMAVORE: Seasons Made to Drift studies and demonstrates instances that help identify new seasons in action. Exhausted (2021) undoes the tales of soil and human fertility from the Neolithic age in the so-called Fertile Crescent, to explore the crisis of infertility and the subsequent expansion of IVF facilities and treatments in contemporary Istanbul.

The exhibition starts with one of five commissioned works, Weathered (2021) on the ground floor of SALT Beyoğlu, where the Forum becomes a “prosthetic” forest of material records of historic droughts and famines in Anatolia. Ranging from newspaper cuttings and poems to fossil leaves, tree rings, and timber fragments, the artefacts refer to climate information from the times when meteorological data was not yet systematically collected.
Traces of Escapees (2021) dives into the sea to diagnose the pollution caused by fish farms and the subsequent genetic erosion of local types.
The Lasting Pond (2021) digs into the shrinking of wetlands on the periphery of Istanbul by tracking water buffalos along their wallowing routes.

Emirhan Altuner is an Istanbul-based exhibition designer, scenographer and researcher with ten years of experience in cultural institutions. He is the Spatial Design and Production Manager at SALT, where he has been actively involved for the research, design, production, and installation since 2016. Working across both archival material and contemporary art, he develops spatial narratives through temporary structures, graphic systems, and adaptive reuse. Alongside his design practice, he initiated Trash in 2026, the program built from exhibition remnants accumulated over fifteen years of SALT's history, accompanied by a series of talks and workshops. The project extends his ongoing interest in alternative modes of circulating knowledge and material resources generated through exhibition-making. Holding both bachelor's and master's degrees from the Istanbul Technical University (ITU), Faculty of Architecture, his master's thesis, Aurama: A Kind of Optic Assistant in the Fiction-Space, explores the physical and conceptual production of fictive spaces through film, theater, exhibition, and scenography from cinematographic and theoretical perspectives. He has been teaching at the Architectural Drawing Studio at Istanbul Bilgi University since 2023. He was recognized as one of Turkey's Young Architects Under 40 by The Circle in 2023.

The exhibition explores the unpublished sections of the Istanbul Encyclopedia, the lifelong undertaking of historian and novelist Reşad Ekrem Koçu. Through drafts, notes, collages, drawings, and archival documents, the exhibition reveals Koçu’s idiosyncratic approach to historiography and his ambition to create a “grand register” of Istanbul.

Taking SALT Galata and its surroundings as a point of departure, the exhibition focuses on the overlooked inhabitants, marginal figures, and forgotten stories that populate Koçu’s archive. Rather than revisiting official narratives of the city, it uncovers an alternative urban history shaped by anecdotes, fragments, and lives that remained beyond the conventional historical record.

Both the poster and the plexiglass inscriptions refer to the characters that unfold throughout the building as a series of encyclopedic entries. The color scheme corresponds to the different chapters of the exhibition. Borrowing from the characters, places, and narratives of the encyclopedia, the exhibition is organized around seven thematic constellations, each distinguished by a specific atmospheric color.

Focusing on the traditions and attire of Istanbul, these entries reveal the everyday lives of the city’s inhabitants through objects, textures, and sounds. Distributed across the first floor, they are presented within a yellow atmosphere inspired by the encyclopedia entry Sunburn in Istanbul. The yellow atmosphere originates from the filtered glass and gradually spills into the ground floor, becoming a defining welcoming element of the exhibition.

At the center of the space, the Table for Imagination invites visitors to create their own characters through techniques of copying and collage, echoing Reşad Ekrem Koçu’s inventive approach to image-making in the Istanbul Encyclopedia.

The Istanbul Encyclopedia pays particular attention to the lives of the city’s marginalized inhabitants. Entries often begin by describing the physical characteristics of a street, avenue, or neighborhood—their buildings, shops, and urban fabric—before unfolding into stories of crimes, scandals, and curiosities that once captured the imagination of Istanbul’s residents.

The exhibition begins with these characters and the nightlife of Istanbul. Spread across the first three chapters, the entries are presented within an atmosphere of blue and purple hues inspired by the nocturnal world of the encyclopedia.

Paper, together with light, is one of the most essential components of the exhibition design. The encyclopedia entries, along with their images and translations, flow across these paper surfaces as a graphic field, unfolding throughout the building. Fragile yet self-supporting, these continuous surfaces weave through the building, guiding visitors while unfolding the archive as a spatial experience.

Exhibition design and scenography for One and the Many, a research-based exhibition exploring the production and circulation of industrial objects in Turkey between 1955 and 1995. Focusing on everyday artifacts from the 1980s, the exhibition traces how industrialization, consumer culture, and infrastructures shaped the material landscape of the period. Bringing together objects, archival materials, and stories from industries ranging from automotive to furniture, textiles, and food production, the exhibition examines the notion of “genuine copies” and reconsiders imitation, adaptation, and reproduction as forms of learning and production within Turkey’s industrial history.

As part of the exhibition, an ongoing research project materialized as Home-Section, a four-metre-long interactive drawing depicting an imaginary apartment in Turkey in 1987. Framed as a technical section drawing, the work reconstructs the domestic landscape of the 1980s through furniture, appliances, consumer goods, and everyday objects characteristic of the period. By distancing the material environment through the conventions of architectural representation, Home-Section offers an alternative way of reading the exhibition’s research. Objects drawn from catalogues, advertisements, photographs, and interviews coexist within a single cross-section, creating a speculative archive of everyday life in 1980s Turkey. An online version of Home-Section can be explored here.

Phase 2 and Phase 3 of the 39th EVA International formed part of a three-phase exhibition programme unfolding across multiple venues in Limerick and online. Bringing together 28 presentations throughout the two phases by Irish and international artists, the programme expanded across venues including Limerick City Gallery of Art, Park Point, Sailor’s Home, and spacecraft. The Guest Programme, Little did they know, was curated by Merve Elveren.

The 39th EVA International took its reference from the “Golden Vein,” a 19th-century descriptor for the agricultural bounty of the Limerick region, and across all phases of the programme it sought to question ideas of land and its contested values in the context of Ireland today. Through the work of the participating artists, these questions extended to broader considerations of how we relate to land in terms of ideology, identity, and resource.

In collaboration with the Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw, Into the Unknown explores how artists have revisited histories, archives, and collective memory following the dissolution of the Eastern Bloc after 1989. Bringing together moving image works, experimental films, and archival projects, the exhibition examines the tensions between official histories and personal narratives, documentary truth and fiction, ideology and everyday life.

Borrowing from the exhibition’s notion of unknownness, the design deliberately fragments visibility throughout the space. Existing architectural elements and temporary interventions alternately reveal and conceal the works, inviting visitors to navigate around structures and materials as they gradually encounter the moving image.

The exhibition opens with a large-scale video installation by Diane Severin Nguyen positioned among the building’s columns, introducing both the spatial logic of partial visibility and the colored light interventions that unfold throughout the exhibition.

Drawing their colors directly from the films, circular graphic elements evoke both the exhibition’s layered narratives and the camera lens as a device of framing, mediation, and perception. Although typography plays a significant role within the exhibition, the exclusive use of lowercase sans-serif letterforms introduces a deliberately neutral and timeless graphic language, allowing the moving image to remain the primary focus.

The notion of “unknownness” takes material form through polycarbonate surfaces and semi-transparent curtains distributed across the upper floors. By distorting light, and moving images, these elements produce moments of partial visibility, allowing visitors to encounter fragmented traces of the works before arriving at the screens themselves.

The exhibition design goes beyond the building's current form with a series of angular layouts. Along with the polycarbonate surfaces, these design choices challenge familiar views and encourage visitors to create their own paths through the exhibition instead of following a set route.
As a final design element, colored light filters taken from the moving images spread their atmospheres into the gallery, guiding visitors through the exhibition.

The exhibition continues at SALT Galata with Enthusiasts Archive by Neil Cummings and Marysia Lewandowska, extending the exhibition’s spatial language through colored light filters and translucent polycarbonate surfaces.

Exhibition design, scenography, and production for Breaking Through A Dam, an exhibition centers on the relationship between landscape, memory, and archives in the formation of this shared ground: Dams, canals, oil wells, geothermal plants, surveillance systems, and cell towers not only transform the surrounding terrain; they also reshape the cultural and social bonds forged around them. Yet collective memory does not cease to exist; rather, it becomes inscribed onto the landscape. Rivers, wetlands, streets, and coffeehouses each serve as an archive that holds this memory.

Exhibition design, scenography, and production for Subsoil by artist Onur Gökmen. The exhibition investigates a largely overlooked episode in Turkey’s environmental and institutional history: the radioactive contamination detected in Black Sea tea following the 1986 Chernobyl disaster. Drawing on research conducted by a group of scientists at Middle East Technical University, including the artist’s parents İnci and Ali Gökmen, the exhibition examines the tensions between scientific evidence, public health, media representation, and state narratives. While reports identified radioactive contamination in tea produced in the region, official responses often downplayed its significance, allowing contaminated products to remain in circulation. Tea subsequently emerged as a material witness to an invisible environmental crisis and its lasting place in collective memory. Combining documentary and fictional elements, the exhibition unfolds through three interconnected scenes. A reconstruction of the METU laboratory where contamination was first measured is accompanied by a documentary based on the testimonies of İnci and Ali Gökmen. A television studio installation examines the role of media in shaping public perception of the crisis, while a short film revisits the narratives that obscured its consequences. Behind these staged environments, a third layer of photographs traces the enduring presence of Chernobyl in Turkey. Together, these fragments reveal how invisible forms of environmental damage continue to shape public health, political discourse, and collective memory across generations.

Exhibition design, scenography, and production for Epipe, the culmination of an oral history and archival research project by Güneş Terkol, developed in collaboration with her mother Elmira Terkol since 2002. The work traces the multi-stage migration of Kazan Tatars from Russia to China and later to Türkiye, bringing together drawing, animation, and embroidery to construct a layered narrative around migration routes, family memory, and intergenerational exchange.

Exhibition design, scenography, and production for We’ve Been at the Tapestry Studio Since the 90s, an exhibition exploring the unique pedagogical model developed within the Tapestry Studio at Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University. Focusing on the studio’s transformation from the 1990s onward under the influence of artist and educator Gülçin Aksoy, the exhibition traces its role as a space of collective learning, artistic experimentation, and alternative forms of knowledge production. Bringing together artworks, archival materials, publications, performances, and personal testimonies, the exhibition examines the connections forged between academia, everyday life, feminist networks, and Istanbul’s independent art scene. In doing so, it reveals an intergenerational community shaped through collaboration, shared practices, and creative dissent.

Exhibition design, visual communication, and production for Translated into Socialism, an exhibition exploring the little-known history of the Turkish-speaking community in Yugoslavia, particularly in Kosovo and Macedonia. Spanning from the 1920s to the late 1980s, the exhibition examines how Turkish identity was negotiated, transformed, and reimagined within the multinational framework of socialist Yugoslavia. Bringing together historical materials from private archives and public collections alongside contemporary artworks, the exhibition traces the cultural, educational, and political initiatives that emerged in the Turkish language under socialism.

Exhibition design, scenography, and production for In the Realm of Three Inland Seas, the most comprehensive survey of Handan Börüteçene’s artistic practice to date. Bringing together works spanning over four decades, the exhibition traces the artist’s enduring engagement with archaeology, history, mythology, and the natural landscapes of Anatolia and Thrace. Featuring early installations, sculptures, notebooks, archival materials, and large-scale works, the exhibition explores recurring themes in Börüteçene’s practice, including the dialogue between past and present, cultural continuity, and what the artist describes as the “memory of the Earth.” At the same time, it reflects on questions of preservation, loss, and the fragile afterlives of artworks and cultural heritage.

Exhibition design, and production for The Skin, Body, and I, the most comprehensive survey of İpek Duben’s work to date, spanning more than four decades of artistic practice. Bringing together paintings, drawings, installations, artist books, and multimedia works, the exhibition traces the artist’s sustained engagement with gender, identity, migration, displacement, violence, and the politics of representation. Structured around the body as both subject and medium, the exhibition follows Duben’s evolving practice from the early 1980s to the present day. Through a selection of key works and series, it reveals her ongoing investigation of personal and collective histories, while reflecting on broader social and political transformations across different geographies and generations.
